intro.why: Every architecture later in the course (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) is trained with exactly this forward pass, loss, backpropagation and update loop. Getting the matrix shapes and the chain rule right here makes the rest mechanical.
prereq: Linear and logistic regression as single neurons (DNN Modules 3–4)

symbols: number of layers (hidden + output; input not counted)
column vector of $B$ ones (broadcasts the bias)

sections.title: Linear limits and the XOR problem
sections.plain: One neuron draws one line; XOR needs two lines combined.
sections.body:
A linear model is a single neuron with activation $f$:

$$\hat y=f(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x+b)\qquad\text{(Eq. 1)}$$

Many relationships are non-linear (pixels → class, words → sentiment, symptoms → disease probability, board → move), and linear models cannot solve non-linearly separable problems (p.4).

$x_1$$x_2$XOR
000
011
101
110

For a single neuron $\hat y=\sigma(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b)$ (Eq. 2), the decision boundary $w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b=0$ is a line. Any monotone $\sigma$ thresholds the same affine function, so the activation choice does not help.

Proof that no line works. Suppose class 1 ⇔ $w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b>0$. From (0,1) and (1,0): $w_2+b>0$ and $w_1+b>0$, sum $w_1+w_2+2b>0$. From (0,0) and (1,1): $b\le0$ and $w_1+w_2+b\le0$, sum $w_1+w_2+2b\le0$. Contradiction.

An MLP solves it (p.7–8)

Architecture 2 → 2 → 1. Each hidden unit learns a linear separator; the output combines them; the non-linearity makes the combined boundary non-linear. Beyond the slides One exact solution with ReLU:

$$h_1=\text{ReLU}(x_1+x_2),\quad h_2=\text{ReLU}(x_1+x_2-1),\quad \hat y=h_1-2h_2$$

Inputs map to $(h_1,h_2)$ = (0,0), (1,0), (1,0), (2,1), giving $\hat y$ = 0, 1, 1, 0. In hidden space the classes are separable by a line, which is exactly the "input space → hidden space" picture on p.8.

sections.title: Non-linearity, and why linear layers collapse
sections.plain: Without bends, many layers equal one layer.
sections.body:
Definition. $f$ is non-linear if it violates linearity for some scalars and inputs:

$$f(a x_1+b x_2)\ne a f(x_1)+b f(x_2)\qquad\text{(Eq. 3)}$$

Collapse. With identity activations, two layers give $\mathbf h^{(2)}=(\mathbf x\mathbf W^{(1)}+\mathbf b^{(1)})\mathbf W^{(2)}+\mathbf b^{(2)}=\mathbf x\underbrace{\mathbf W^{(1)}\mathbf W^{(2)}}_{\mathbf W'}+\underbrace{\mathbf b^{(1)}\mathbf W^{(2)}+\mathbf b^{(2)}}_{\mathbf b'}$: a single affine layer. By induction any depth collapses. Non-linear activations prevent this and let depth add expressive power (p.10).

sections.title: Activation functions and their derivatives
sections.plain: Each activation is a different bend; its slope controls how well blame flows back.
sections.body:
$$\sigma(z)=\frac1{1+e^{-z}},\quad \sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\qquad\text{(Eq. 46)}$$ $$\tanh(z)=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}},\quad \tanh'(z)=1-\tanh^2(z)\qquad\text{(Eq. 47)}$$ $$\text{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z),\quad \text{ReLU}'(z)=\begin{cases}1&z>0\\0&z\le0\end{cases}\qquad\text{(Eq. 48)}$$

Derivation of Eq. 46. $\sigma'(z)=\frac{e^{-z}}{(1+e^{-z})^2}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$. Its maximum is $0.25$ at $z=0$.

Property (p.12)SigmoidTanhReLULeaky ReLU
Range(0, 1)(−1, 1)[0, ∞)(−∞, ∞)
Zero-centredNoYesNoMarked yes on the slide*
DifferentiableYesYesNot at 0Not at 0
Vanishing gradientHighModerateNo (for z > 0)No
Compute costHighHighLowLow
Typical useOutput layerHidden layerHidden layerHidden layer

*Leaky ReLU outputs are mostly non-negative, so it is closer to zero-centred than ReLU but not truly zero-centred. Flagged for review.

Why ReLU works well (p.13): cheap (a comparison, no exponentials); gradient exactly 1 for $z>0$, so it does not shrink through layers; sparse activation (many units output 0). Caveat: dying ReLU. A unit whose $z\le0$ for all inputs has zero gradient forever. Fixes: Leaky ReLU $\max(\alpha z,z)$ with small $\alpha$ (e.g. 0.01), PReLU (learned $\alpha$), ELU.

sections.title: The four components of a DFNN
sections.body:
A DFNN has one or more hidden layers between input and output; information flows forward through non-linear transformations. A complete system needs (p.15):

  1. Data: input features and target outputs.
  2. Model: multi-layer architecture with non-linear activations.
  3. Objective: a loss function to minimise.
  4. Learning algorithm: backpropagation with gradient descent.

This is the same framework as the linear models, with added depth and non-linearity.

sections.title: Data and mini-batch representation
sections.plain: Stack examples as rows of a matrix.
sections.body:
$$\mathcal D=\{(\mathbf x^{(i)},\mathbf y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{N}\quad\text{(Eq. 4)}\qquad \mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{N\times d}\ \text{(rows } \mathbf x^{(i)\top})\quad\text{(Eq. 5)}\qquad \mathbf Y\in\mathbb R^{N\times K}\quad\text{(Eq. 6)}$$

$K=1$ for regression, $K=C$ for $C$-class classification.

$$\mathcal B=\{(\mathbf x^{(i)},\mathbf y^{(i)})\}_{i\in\text{batch}}\ \text{(Eq. 7)},\qquad \mathbf X_\mathcal B\in\mathbb R^{B\times d}\ \text{(Eq. 8)},\qquad \mathbf Y_\mathcal B\in\mathbb R^{B\times K}\ \text{(Eq. 9)}$$

Common $B\in\{32,64,128,256\}$: a balance between computational efficiency and gradient stability, and it parallelises on GPUs.

sections.title: Architecture, layer computation and parameter count
sections.plain: Each layer: multiply by weights, add bias, apply activation.
sections.body:
For $\ell=1,\dots,L$ (p.19):

$$\mathbf W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell-1}\times n_\ell}\ \text{(Eq. 10)},\quad \mathbf b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}\ \text{(Eq. 11)},\quad \mathbf h^{(0)}=\mathbf x\ \text{(Eq. 12)}$$ $$\mathbf z^{(\ell)}=\mathbf h^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell)}+\mathbf b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}\ \text{(Eq. 13)},\qquad \mathbf h^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(\mathbf z^{(\ell)})\ \text{(Eq. 14)},\qquad \hat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf h^{(L)}\ \text{(Eq. 15)}$$

Vectorised over a mini-batch (p.20)

$$\mathbf H^{(0)}=\mathbf X_\mathcal B\ \text{(Eq. 16)},\quad \mathbf Z^{(\ell)}=\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell)}+\mathbf 1_B\mathbf b^{(\ell)\top}\in\mathbb R^{B\times n_\ell}\ \text{(Eq. 17)}$$ $$\mathbf H^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(\mathbf Z^{(\ell)})\ \text{(Eq. 18)},\qquad \hat{\mathbf Y}_\mathcal B=\mathbf H^{(L)}\in\mathbb R^{B\times K}\ \text{(Eq. 19)}$$

Shape check: $(B\times n_{\ell-1})(n_{\ell-1}\times n_\ell)=B\times n_\ell$; $\mathbf 1_B\mathbf b^\top$ copies the bias into every row.

Parameters (p.21)

$$\text{Params}^{(\ell)}=n_{\ell-1}n_\ell+n_\ell=n_\ell(n_{\ell-1}+1)\ \text{(Eq. 20)},\qquad \text{Total}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}n_\ell(n_{\ell-1}+1)\ \text{(Eq. 21)}$$

Worked example 784 → 256 → 128 → 10: $784\cdot256+256=200{,}960$; $256\cdot128+128=32{,}896$; $128\cdot10+10=1{,}290$; total $235{,}146$ (verified in code below and in the counter).

sections.title: Loss functions and the objective
sections.plain: Pick the loss that matches the output type.
sections.body:
$$\text{MSE: }\ell(\hat{\mathbf y},\mathbf y)=\tfrac12\lVert\hat{\mathbf y}-\mathbf y\rVert^2=\tfrac12\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\hat y_k-y_k)^2\qquad\text{(Eq. 22)}$$ $$\text{BCE: }\ell(\hat y,y)=-[y\log\hat y+(1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]\qquad\text{(Eq. 23)}$$ $$\text{CCE: }\ell(\hat{\mathbf y},\mathbf y)=-\sum_{k=1}^{C}y_k\log\hat y_k\qquad\text{(Eq. 24)}$$

For CCE, $\mathbf y$ is one-hot and $\hat{\mathbf y}=\text{softmax}(\mathbf z)$ with $\text{softmax}(\mathbf z)_k=\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^{C}e^{z_j}}$ (p.50).

$$\ell^{(i)}=\ell(\hat{\mathbf y}^{(i)},\mathbf y^{(i)})\ \text{(Eq. 25/35)},\qquad J(\mathbf W,\mathbf b)=\frac1B\sum_{i\in\mathcal B}\ell^{(i)}\ \text{(Eq. 26/36)},\qquad \mathbf W^*,\mathbf b^*=\arg\min_{\mathbf W,\mathbf b}J\ \text{(Eq. 27)}$$

where $\mathbf W=\{\mathbf W^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf W^{(L)}\}$ and $\mathbf b$ likewise. Why cross-entropy for classification? It is the negative log-likelihood of a Bernoulli/categorical model, so minimising it is maximum likelihood; and paired with sigmoid/softmax its gradient does not saturate (next sections).

sections.title: Mini-batch SGD and the full training algorithm
sections.plain: Forward, loss, backward, update, repeated over mini-batches.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf W^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\mathbf W^{(\ell)}-\eta\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf W^{(\ell)}}\ \text{(Eq. 28)},\qquad \mathbf b^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\mathbf b^{(\ell)}-\eta\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf b^{(\ell)}}\ \text{(Eq. 29)}$$

The challenge is computing these gradients efficiently; backpropagation is the answer (p.24).

ALGORITHM 1+2: DFNN TRAINING WITH MINI-BATCH SGD   (slides p.25–26)
Input: D, sizes (n0..nL), η, B, epochs T
for ℓ = 1..L: W(ℓ) ← random(n_{ℓ-1} × n_ℓ);  b(ℓ) ← 0
for t = 1..T
    shuffle D
    for each mini-batch (X_B, Y_B) of size B
        # forward
        H(0) ← X_B
        for ℓ = 1..L:  Z(ℓ) ← H(ℓ-1) W(ℓ) + 1_B b(ℓ)ᵀ ;  H(ℓ) ← σ(ℓ)(Z(ℓ))
        Ŷ ← H(L);  J ← (1/B) Σ ℓ(ŷ(i), y(i))
        # backward
        δ(L) ← Ŷ − Y                             # per-example signal for matched loss/activation pairs
        for ℓ = L-1..1:  δ(ℓ) ← (δ(ℓ+1) W(ℓ+1)ᵀ) ⊙ σ'(ℓ)(Z(ℓ))
        for ℓ = 1..L:    ∂J/∂W(ℓ) ← (1/B) H(ℓ-1)ᵀ δ(ℓ) ;  ∂J/∂b(ℓ) ← (1/B) 1_Bᵀ δ(ℓ)
        # update
        for ℓ = 1..L:    W(ℓ) ← W(ℓ) − η ∂J/∂W(ℓ) ;  b(ℓ) ← b(ℓ) − η ∂J/∂b(ℓ)

The 1/B factor is applied exactly once, in the gradient lines. The slides apply it twice; see the review note in the backprop section.

sections.title: Forward propagation
sections.plain: Run the layers in order and keep the intermediate values for backprop.
sections.body:
ALGORITHM 3: FORWARD PROPAGATION   (p.29)
Input: x ∈ R^d, {W(ℓ), b(ℓ)}
h(0) ← x
for ℓ = 1..L
    z(ℓ) ← h(ℓ-1) W(ℓ) + b(ℓ)        # linear transformation
    h(ℓ) ← σ(ℓ)(z(ℓ))                 # non-linear activation (store for backprop)
return ŷ = h(L), {h(ℓ), z(ℓ)}
$$\mathbf H^{(0)}=\mathbf X_\mathcal B\ \text{(Eq. 30)},\quad \mathbf Z^{(\ell)}=\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell)}+\mathbf 1_B\mathbf b^{(\ell)\top}\ \text{(Eq. 31)},\quad \mathbf H^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(\mathbf Z^{(\ell)})\ \text{(Eq. 32)},\quad \hat{\mathbf Y}_\mathcal B=\mathbf H^{(L)}\ \text{(Eq. 33)}$$ $$\text{Cost per forward pass: }O\Big(B\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}n_{\ell-1}n_\ell\Big)\qquad\text{(Eq. 34)}$$

The matrix products dominate; activations add only $O(B\sum n_\ell)$. All $\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}$ and $\mathbf H^{(\ell)}$ must be stored for the backward pass, so training memory is $O(B\sum_\ell n_\ell)$ on top of the parameters.

sections.title: Backpropagation: full derivation
sections.plain: The chain rule applied layer by layer, from the output back to the input.
sections.body:
Error signal. Define $\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}=\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}}\in\mathbb R^{B\times n_\ell}$ (Eq. 39). Backprop has two steps: propagate $\boldsymbol\delta^{(L)}\to\boldsymbol\delta^{(L-1)}\to\dots\to\boldsymbol\delta^{(1)}$, then turn each into parameter gradients.

1. Output layer (p.32)

$$\boldsymbol\delta^{(L)}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf Z^{(L)}}\in\mathbb R^{B\times K}\ \text{(Eq. 37)},\qquad \boldsymbol\delta^{(L)}=\frac1B(\hat{\mathbf Y}-\mathbf Y)\ \text{(Eq. 38)}$$

for all three matched pairs: MSE + identity, BCE + sigmoid, CCE + softmax. Beyond the slides Why the same form:

  • MSE + identity: $\ell=\frac12(\hat y-y)^2$, $\hat y=z$ ⇒ $\partial\ell/\partial z=\hat y-y$.
  • BCE + sigmoid: $\partial\ell/\partial\hat y=\frac{\hat y-y}{\hat y(1-\hat y)}$ and $\partial\hat y/\partial z=\hat y(1-\hat y)$; the product is $\hat y-y$. The sigmoid's saturation cancels exactly.
  • CCE + softmax: $\partial\hat y_j/\partial z_k=\hat y_j(\mathbb 1[j=k]-\hat y_k)$, so $\partial\ell/\partial z_k=-\sum_j\frac{y_j}{\hat y_j}\hat y_j(\mathbb 1[j=k]-\hat y_k)=\hat y_k\sum_jy_j-y_k=\hat y_k-y_k$.

Averaging over the batch adds the $\frac1B$.

2. Hidden layers (p.34)

$$\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf H^{(\ell)}}\frac{\partial\mathbf H^{(\ell)}}{\partial\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}}\ \text{(Eq. 40)}$$ $$\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf H^{(\ell)}}=\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf Z^{(\ell+1)}}\frac{\partial\mathbf Z^{(\ell+1)}}{\partial\mathbf H^{(\ell)}}=\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell+1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell+1)\top}\ \text{(Eq. 41)},\qquad \frac{\partial\mathbf H^{(\ell)}}{\partial\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}}=\sigma'^{(\ell)}(\mathbf Z^{(\ell)})\ \text{(Eq. 42, element-wise)}$$ $$\boxed{\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}=\left(\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell+1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell+1)\top}\right)\odot\sigma'^{(\ell)}(\mathbf Z^{(\ell)})}\qquad\text{(Eq. 43)}$$

Shapes: $(B\times n_{\ell+1})(n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell)=B\times n_\ell$, matching $\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}$. Because the activation is element-wise its Jacobian is diagonal, which is why it becomes a Hadamard product.

3. Parameter gradients (p.35)

Since $\mathbf Z^{(\ell)}=\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell)}+\mathbf 1_B\mathbf b^{(\ell)\top}$:

$$\frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf W^{(\ell)}}=\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell-1}\times n_\ell},\qquad \frac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf b^{(\ell)}}=\mathbf 1_B^\top\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}$$

The slides write these as $\frac1B\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}$ (Eq. 44) and $\frac1B\mathbf 1_B^\top\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}$ (Eq. 45). The same error signal is shared by the weight and bias gradients.

Review flag: the 1/B factor appears twice in the slides. Eq. 38 already puts $\frac1B$ inside $\boldsymbol\delta^{(L)}$, and Eq. 44–45 apply $\frac1B$ again, which would scale the gradient by $1/B^2$. Use one or the other. Either define $\boldsymbol\delta^{(L)}=\hat{\mathbf Y}-\mathbf Y$ per example and keep the $\frac1B$ in Eq. 44–45 (the convention in the code below), or keep Eq. 38 and drop the $\frac1B$ from Eq. 44–45.
ALGORITHM 4: BACKPROPAGATION   (p.36, consistent 1/B)
δ(L) ← (Ŷ − Y)                                  # per-example signals, B × K
for ℓ = L−1 .. 1:   δ(ℓ) ← (δ(ℓ+1) W(ℓ+1)ᵀ) ⊙ σ'(ℓ)(Z(ℓ))
for ℓ = 1 .. L:     ∂J/∂W(ℓ) ← (1/B) H(ℓ−1)ᵀ δ(ℓ) ;   ∂J/∂b(ℓ) ← (1/B) 1_Bᵀ δ(ℓ)
return all gradients

The lab below runs every step on a 2‑2‑1 network with real numbers and checks each gradient against a finite-difference estimate.

sections.title: Why backpropagation is efficient
sections.plain: One backward pass gets every gradient, instead of one pass per weight.
sections.body:
Naive approach: estimate each $\partial J/\partial w_{ij}^{(\ell)}$ separately (e.g. finite differences). That needs a forward pass per parameter: $O(P\times C_{forward})$, intractable for millions of parameters.

Backprop reuses intermediate results: one forward plus one backward pass, $O(C_{forward}+C_{backward})\approx2\times O(C_{forward})$. The backward pass has the same order of cost as the forward pass. Speed-up ≈ $P/2$ (e.g. ~100,000× for $P=200{,}000$). It is dynamic programming over the chain rule: each $\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}$ is computed once and reused by every parameter that depends on it.

Beyond the slides This is reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX implement. Finite differences remain useful as a gradient check (see the lab and code).

sections.title: Parameter update step
sections.plain: Move every weight a little against its gradient.
sections.body:
For a single example (row-vector form):

$$\mathbf W^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\mathbf W^{(\ell)}-\eta\,\mathbf h^{(\ell-1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}\ \text{(Eq. 49)},\qquad \mathbf b^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\mathbf b^{(\ell)}-\eta\,\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}\ \text{(Eq. 50)}$$

$\mathbf h^{(\ell-1)\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{(\ell)}$ is an outer product of shape $n_{\ell-1}\times n_\ell$: weight $w_{ij}$ changes in proportion to "how active input $i$ was" × "how much output $j$ was to blame". With $\eta>0$ this moves parameters in the direction that reduces the loss.

sections.title: Prediction with a trained network
sections.plain: Prediction is just the forward pass.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf h^{(0)}=\mathbf x_{new};\quad \mathbf z^{(\ell)}=\mathbf h^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell)}+\mathbf b^{(\ell)}\ \text{(Eq. 51)};\quad \mathbf h^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(\mathbf z^{(\ell)})\ \text{(Eq. 52)};\quad \hat{\mathbf y}_{new}=\mathbf h^{(L)}$$

Interpretation: regression → $\hat{\mathbf y}_{new}$ is the value; binary → class 1 if $\hat y_{new}>0.5$; multi-class → $\arg\max_k\hat y_{k,new}$.

$$\mathbf H^{(0)}=\mathbf X_{test}\ \text{(Eq. 53)},\ \mathbf Z^{(\ell)}=\mathbf H^{(\ell-1)}\mathbf W^{(\ell)}+\mathbf 1_{N_{test}}\mathbf b^{(\ell)\top}\ \text{(Eq. 54)},\ \mathbf H^{(\ell)}=\sigma^{(\ell)}(\mathbf Z^{(\ell)})\ \text{(Eq. 55)},\ \hat{\mathbf Y}_{test}=\mathbf H^{(L)}\in\mathbb R^{N_{test}\times K}\ \text{(Eq. 56)}$$

Batch prediction uses efficient matrix operations (GPU), produces all predictions in one forward pass, and is essential for large-scale deployment. At inference nothing needs to be stored for a backward pass.

sections.title: Depth vs width and the Universal Approximation Theorem
sections.plain: Depth gives hierarchy and parameter efficiency.
sections.body:
Depth (more layers): hierarchical features, more expressive, often better generalisation. Width (more units per layer): more parallel features and higher capacity, with a risk of overfitting (p.44).

Hierarchy example for images (p.45): layer 1 edges and colours → layer 2 textures and simple shapes → layer 3 parts (eyes, wheels) → layer 4+ objects (faces, cars). Deep networks can represent exponentially more functions than shallow ones with the same number of parameters.

Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko 1989; Hornik et al. 1989). A feed-forward network with a single hidden layer containing a finite number of neurons can approximate any continuous function on a compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$ to arbitrary accuracy, given an appropriate activation function.

What it means: even shallow networks are powerful in theory, but they may need exponentially many hidden units. Deep networks are far more parameter-efficient, learn better representations, and generalise better in practice (p.46).

Beyond the slides UAT is an existence result. It says nothing about whether gradient descent will find those weights, how much data is needed, or how well the network generalises. "Appropriate" activation means non-polynomial; ReLU qualifies.

sections.title: Challenges with very deep networks
sections.plain: Gradients can fade or blow up as they pass back through many layers.
sections.body:
1. Vanishing gradients: gradients become exponentially small in early layers, which then fail to learn useful features. Solutions: ReLU, careful initialisation, normalisation.
  2. Exploding gradients: gradients become exponentially large, causing NaN/Inf. Solutions: gradient clipping, proper initialisation.
  3. Degradation: very deep plain networks are harder to optimise; training error can rise with depth. Solution: residual / skip connections (ResNets).

Beyond the slides Unrolling Eq. 43 across layers, $\boldsymbol\delta^{(1)}$ contains a product of $L-1$ factors of the form $\mathbf W^{(\ell)\top}\text{diag}(\sigma'(\mathbf z^{(\ell)}))$. With sigmoid, $\sigma'\le0.25$, so if weights are $O(1)$ the signal shrinks roughly like $0.25^{L}$: after 10 layers about $10^{-6}$. If weight norms exceed $1/\max\sigma'$ the product grows instead. The activation-derivative lab shows this product as you vary depth.

sections.title: Architecture design
sections.plain: Match the output to the task, use ReLU inside, start small.
sections.body:
Key decisions (p.49): number of layers $L$, units per layer, activation per layer, output layer, regularisation. No universal answer; it depends on problem, data and compute.

Task (p.50)Output unitsOutput activationLoss
Regression$K$ = output dimensionIdentityMSE
Binary classification1SigmoidBCE
Multi-class ($C$)$C$SoftmaxCCE

General guidelines (p.51): start simple (2–3 hidden layers, 10–100 units) and grow if needed; common patterns are decreasing width $n_1>n_2>\dots$ (funnel), constant width, or hourglass (wide → narrow → wide, for compressed representations); more data supports larger networks.

Hidden activation (p.52)When to useAvoid when
ReLUDefault; fast, no vanishing gradientVery deep nets with dying units
Leaky ReLUDeep networks; fixes dying ReLURarely a bad choice
TanhSmall networks; zero-centredVery deep nets (vanishing gradient)
SigmoidBinary output onlyHidden layers (strong saturation)

Regularisation (p.53): L2 (weight decay), dropout, early stopping, batch normalisation; covered in Modules 10 and 11.

sections.title: Initialisation, hyperparameters, preprocessing and debugging
sections.plain: Random init, standardised inputs, watch both losses, check gradients.
sections.body:
Initialisation (p.55): zero initialisation is bad; random is good: Xavier/Glorot for sigmoid/tanh, He for ReLU; biases to zero. Beyond the slides Zero weights make every unit in a layer compute the same output and receive the same gradient, so they stay identical (symmetry). Xavier draws with variance $\frac{2}{n_{in}+n_{out}}$; He uses $\frac{2}{n_{in}}$. Both keep activation variance roughly constant across layers.

Hyperparameters (p.56): learning rate $\eta\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1\}$ (or Adam with 0.001); batch size 32–256 (larger is faster but may generalise worse, limited by GPU memory); epochs with early stopping on validation loss, typically 50–200 for moderate datasets.

Preprocessing (p.57): standardise (recommended) or min-max scale, applying the training-set transform to validation and test; impute missing values or add indicator variables; one-hot nominal and ordinal-encode ordered categories.

Monitoring (p.58): training loss should fall steadily; validation loss falls then plateaus or rises (stop there); track accuracy and gradient norms.

Symptom (p.59)DiagnosisFix
Loss = NaN/InfNumerical instabilityLower η, check gradients, normalise inputs
Loss not decreasingη too small or a bugRaise η, verify gradient computation
Loss oscillatingη too largeLower η, use a schedule
Train ↓, validation ↑OverfittingRegularise, dropout, more data
Both highUnderfittingWider/deeper, train longer
Slow convergencePoor init or featuresHe/Xavier, normalise
Gradients → 0VanishingReLU, better init, batch norm
Gradients → ∞ExplodingClipping, lower η

Checklist (p.60): before training check normalisation, train/val/test split, output layer and loss match the task, weights not all zero. During training check that the training loss falls, validation is tracked, gradients are healthy and there are no NaNs. Sanity checks: overfit a small batch to near-zero loss, verify tensor shapes, test the forward pass before adding backprop.

Best practices (p.61): vectorise (never loop over examples); keep forward, loss and backward modular and test each; numerical stability (log-sum-exp for softmax, clip if $\lVert\nabla\rVert>$ threshold, watch for NaN/Inf); reproducibility (seeds, saved hyperparameters, tracked experiments).

sections.title: Summary and what comes next
sections.plain: DFNNs are the foundation for every later architecture.
sections.body:
• Non-linearity is essential; without it deep networks collapse to linear models.
  • DFNN = stacked layers with non-linear activations, enabling hierarchical feature learning.
  • Four components: data, model, objective, learning (backprop + SGD).
  • Backprop efficiently computes gradients with the chain rule.
  • Depth gives hierarchy and expressiveness; width adds capacity but needs more data.
  • Initialisation, normalisation and regularisation are critical; ReLU for hidden layers, task-specific output activations.

Next (p.65): CNNs (images), RNNs (sequences), Transformers (attention), GNNs (graphs); optimisers (Adam, RMSProp, AdaGrad), dropout and batch norm, transfer learning, interpretability, efficient inference. To become proficient (p.66): implement forward and backprop from scratch with gradient checking on XOR/MNIST, then use frameworks, iterate, and study successful architectures.

sections.title: Time and space complexity
sections.body:
StepTimeMemory
Forward pass (batch)$O(B\sum_\ell n_{\ell-1}n_\ell)$ (Eq. 34)$O(B\sum_\ell n_\ell)$ activations kept for backprop
Backward pass≈ same order as forward (two matrix products per layer)gradients: $O(P)$
Update$O(P)$$O(P)$ (more for momentum/Adam states)
Inference$O(N_{test}\sum_\ell n_{\ell-1}n_\ell)$only the current layer's activations

$P=\sum_\ell n_\ell(n_{\ell-1}+1)$ (Eq. 21). One epoch costs about $3\times$ the forward FLOPs times $N/B$ batches.

sections.title: Assumptions and limitations
sections.body:
• Training data is representative of deployment data (i.i.d.); DFNNs extrapolate poorly.
  • Fixed-size, unordered feature vectors: DFNNs ignore spatial structure (use CNNs) and sequence order (use RNNs/Transformers).
  • Non-convex loss: SGD finds a good local minimum, not a guaranteed global one; results depend on initialisation and hyperparameters.
  • Data-hungry relative to linear models or trees on small tabular datasets; often beaten by gradient-boosted trees there.
  • Limited interpretability (see ML Module 11).

sections.title: Comparison with related models

sections.title: Common technical misconceptions
sections.body:
• "The output gradient is always $\hat y-y$." Only for the matched pairs (MSE+identity, BCE+sigmoid, CCE+softmax). MSE with a sigmoid output keeps a $\sigma'$ factor and learns slowly when saturated.
  • "ReLU has no vanishing gradient, so deep ReLU nets always train." Dead units have zero gradient, and products of weight matrices can still explode or vanish without good initialisation.
  • "Backprop is approximate." It is exact (up to floating point); finite differences are the approximation.
  • "UAT means one hidden layer is enough in practice." It guarantees existence, not learnability or efficiency.
  • "Biases need random initialisation too." Zero biases are fine; symmetry is broken by the random weights.
  • "Softmax probabilities are calibrated confidence." Networks are often over-confident; calibration is a separate step.

code.title: A 2‑4‑1 network trained on XOR from scratch, with a gradient check
code.explain: Implements Eq. 13–15 forward, Eq. 43–45 backward (with the consistent 1/B convention), and Eq. 49–50 updates. The last line compares one backprop gradient with a central finite difference.
mistakes: Using δ(L) = (Ŷ−Y)/B and then dividing by B again in the weight gradient.
Forgetting the activation derivative (tanh' = 1 − h²) in hidden layers.
Transposing W the wrong way: check shapes at every line.
code.notes: Always gradient-check a hand-written backward pass on a tiny network before scaling up. This is the slides' 'implement from scratch' advice (p.66).
code.code:
import numpy as np

# XOR: the problem a single neuron cannot solve (slides p.5-8)
X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)   # B x d
Y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]], dtype=float)               # B x K

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
W1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)); b1 = np.zeros(4)                # d -> n1 hidden units
W2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)); b2 = np.zeros(1)                # n1 -> K
sig = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def forward(X):
    Z1 = X @ W1 + b1;  H1 = np.tanh(Z1)                         # hidden layer
    Z2 = H1 @ W2 + b2; Yh = sig(Z2)                             # sigmoid output
    return Z1, H1, Z2, Yh

def bce(Yh, Y):
    return -np.mean(Y * np.log(Yh) + (1 - Y) * np.log(1 - Yh))

eta, B = 0.5, len(X)
for epoch in range(3000):
    Z1, H1, Z2, Yh = forward(X)
    d2 = Yh - Y                              # delta(L) for BCE + sigmoid (per example)
    gW2 = H1.T @ d2 / B; gb2 = d2.mean(0)    # dJ/dW(L) = (1/B) H^T delta
    d1 = (d2 @ W2.T) * (1 - H1**2)           # delta(l) = (delta(l+1) W^T) * tanh'(z)
    gW1 = X.T @ d1 / B;  gb1 = d1.mean(0)
    W2 -= eta * gW2; b2 -= eta * gb2; W1 -= eta * gW1; b1 -= eta * gb1

print("loss:", round(bce(forward(X)[3], Y), 4))
print("predictions:", forward(X)[3].ravel().round(3))

# Gradient check: compare backprop with a finite difference for one weight
eps = 1e-5; i, j = 0, 1
Z1, H1, Z2, Yh = forward(X); d2 = Yh - Y; d1 = (d2 @ W2.T) * (1 - H1**2)
analytic = (X.T @ d1 / B)[i, j]
W1[i, j] += eps; up = bce(forward(X)[3], Y)
W1[i, j] -= 2 * eps; down = bce(forward(X)[3], Y); W1[i, j] += eps
print("grad check:", round(analytic, 8), round((up - down) / (2 * eps), 8))

code.title: Parameter counting
code.explain: Eq. 20–21 applied to the slide's 784‑256‑128‑10 network.
mistakes: Counting the input layer as a layer with parameters.
code.notes: Frameworks report the same: PyTorch's sum of p.numel() gives 235,146 for this architecture.
code.code:
def count_params(sizes):
    """sizes = [n0, n1, ..., nL]; each layer has n_{l-1} * n_l weights + n_l biases."""
    rows = [(l, sizes[l-1], sizes[l], sizes[l] * (sizes[l-1] + 1)) for l in range(1, len(sizes))]
    for l, a, b, p in rows:
        print(f"layer {l}: {a} x {b} + {b} = {p:,}")
    print("total:", f"{sum(r[3] for r in rows):,}")

count_params([784, 256, 128, 10])     # the slide's example (p.21)

code.title: DFNN vs a linear model on a non-linear dataset
code.explain: Two-moons data is not linearly separable. Logistic regression (a single neuron) is compared with a 32‑16 ReLU network trained by mini-batch SGD with early stopping.
code.notes: The gap here is modest because the moons are only mildly tangled; on images or text it is huge.
code.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = make_moons(n_samples=600, noise=0.25, random_state=0)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

linear = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
mlp = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                    MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(32, 16), activation="relu",
                                  solver="sgd", learning_rate_init=0.05, batch_size=32,
                                  max_iter=500, early_stopping=True, random_state=0)).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

print("logistic regression accuracy:", round(linear.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print("DFNN (32-16, ReLU) accuracy: ", round(mlp.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print("trainable parameters:", sum(w.size for w in mlp[-1].coefs_) + sum(b.size for b in mlp[-1].intercepts_))

code.title: The same architecture in PyTorch
code.explain: nn.Linear layers implement Eq. 13; CrossEntropyLoss combines softmax and CCE in a numerically stable way, so its gradient w.r.t. the logits is the Eq. 38 form; loss.backward() runs Algorithm 4.
mistakes: Adding a softmax layer before CrossEntropyLoss (it applies softmax internally).
code.notes: Not executed here (PyTorch was unavailable in the build environment).
code.code:
import torch
from torch import nn

model = nn.Sequential(                 # 784 -> 256 -> 128 -> 10, as on p.21
    nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(128, 10))                # logits; softmax lives inside the loss
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()        # softmax + categorical cross-entropy, numerically stable
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.05)

def train_step(xb, yb):                # xb: B x 784, yb: B class indices
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)      # forward pass + loss
    loss.backward()                    # backpropagation fills .grad for every W, b
    opt.step()                         # W <- W - eta * dJ/dW
    return loss.item()

print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))   # 235146
